title: Theranos – Silicon Valley’s Greatest Disaster
selection_reason: Founder-led fraud built on hype, celebrity board and media; closest structural analogue to Fyre (promise vs. reality). Same topic as MagnatesMedia V-magnates-01 for direct comparison.
narrative_question: How did a company with no working product reach a $9B valuation, and how did it collapse?

hook.summary: News-clip cold open (indictment), aerial San Francisco establishing shots, then narrator states the premise, the money and the ending up front.
hook.promise: The full story of the deceit and how it all came crashing down.

structure.beat: Cold open: news audio + aerials, end revealed
Title card 'Part One – Elizabeth and the rise of Theranos'
Childhood photos, origin, dropout, seed money
How the product was supposed to work (explainer)
'This is the big lie': why it was technically impossible
Escalation: lies, firings, Steve Jobs obsession, board
Walgreens/Safeway deals, Sunny, culture of fear
Ian Gibbons' death (emotional low point)
Peak: $9B valuation, Fortune cover, TED
Part Two title card: 'The truth always wins' – WSJ investigation
Reveal: WSJ article, FDA inspection, lawsuits
Moral reflection: appearance of success
Status at publication, counterfactual question, channel outro

revelations: Tests were run on third-party machines (12:21)
payoff: WSJ exposé and collapse, then a reflective 'why it worked' section; legal outcome stated as of 2019.

visual.method: histogram difference, frames 0.2 s apart, played at 4x; per-minute rate

archival_maps_graphics_3d: Mostly licensed/news archival video and press photos, magazine covers, court/document screenshots with highlighted lines, simple kinetic text ('AND IT'S SMALLER', '$1 Million'), one exploded product diagram; no maps, no 3D.

audio.voice: Single calm male narrator, ~175 wpm, even delivery
audio.music: Continuous ambient/electronic bed (median level -19.5 dB, <6 % quiet); '[Music]' interludes at section turns
audio.ambience: News-clip sound used as diegetic layer in cold open and at the reveal
audio.silence: Almost none; narration gaps ≥3 s only at 1:18, 9:44, 22:50 and the outro
audio.transitions: Black title cards between parts; mostly hard cuts

evidence: Claims anchored by on-screen news clips, magazine covers, quoted documents and deposition excerpts; numbers shown as kinetic text. No on-screen source citations seen in sampled frames.

thumbnail.composition: Current thumbnail: tight portrait of Holmes right, bold condensed white/red title 'THERANOS – THE FULL MOVIE' left on hot-pink field.
thumbnail.title_relation: Thumbnail text differs from the title (thumbnail appears to have been updated later; title kept).

works: States the ending first, then asks how — curiosity survives a known outcome
Two-part structure with title cards gives the viewer a map
Steady archival density keeps a faceless 24-min video moving
improve: Many claims carry no visible source on screen
Long middle section is a list of incidents with similar intensity
Outro promo for other videos breaks the reflective ending
transfer: Cold open with real news audio of the fall, then rewind to the beginning
Part title cards for a 2–3 act story
Explain the 'big lie' technically in plain terms before the fall

title: Theranos: The Most Evil Business In The World
selection_reason: Same subject as V-coldfusion-01 made three years later in a faster, more stylised register; part 1 of a mini-series, useful for cliffhanger/series structure.
topic: Theranos, part 1 (founding to retail launch and fame)
narrative_question: How did Holmes scam her way to the top, and how did she get away with it?

hook.summary: Founder's own slogan as audio, then a childhood anecdote ('I want to be a billionaire'), the rise in one breath, and the twist 'it was all a lie'.
hook.promise: Why and how she scammed her way to the top and how it all came crashing down.

structure.beat: Cold open: subject's own quote + childhood ambition + 'it was all a lie'
Founding, name, finger-prick vision
Prototype and how it was supposed to work
First deception: fake demos for investors
Firing the CFO, invented forecasts
Culture of fear: Sunny, surveillance, NDAs
Mid-roll sponsor
Walgreens/Safeway launch: turning point – public now at risk
How the stores really worked (third-party machines, FedEx)
Peak: Forbes billionaire; question 'how was she getting away with this' -> part 2

revelations: Investor demos were faked by lab staff (3:04)
payoff: No payoff in this part: ends on an open question that sends viewers to part 2.

visual.method: histogram difference, frames 0.2 s apart, played at 4x; per-minute rate

archival_maps_graphics_3d: Heavy use of what appears to be dramatised TV/film footage (actors), plus press photos and stock lab b-roll, all graded into one red/black look with animated red ink blots; keyword title cards; no maps or 3D.

audio.voice: One male narrator, ~196 wpm, conversational and fast, rhetorical questions
audio.music: Continuous bed (median about -17.5 dB, 0 % quiet in all windows)
audio.ambience: Short interview clips from former employees as voice inserts
audio.silence: Narration gaps ≥3 s only at 0:43 and around the sponsor break
audio.transitions: Ink-blot wipes and chapter cards ('The Secrets')

evidence: Inserted interview audio from former employees supports key claims; numbers on kinetic text cards; no visible source citations.

thumbnail.composition: Face of subject left with exaggerated wide eyes, red ink splash, blood vial, one word 'FRAUD' in dripping red letters on white.
thumbnail.title_relation: Thumbnail gives the verdict (FRAUD); title gives a superlative ('most evil business').

works: Opens with the subject's own words, then contradicts them
One strong colour motif ties every source type together
Keyword cards repeat the narration noun so the image always says what the voice says
improve: Dramatised footage from fiction blurs fact and re-enactment and is a rights risk
Superlative title ('most evil') reads as clickbait for a verified story
transfer: Open with the subject's own promise and cut to reality
A theme colour derived from the story (for Fyre: fire/sunset orange vs. grey tent reality)
Keyword cards for names and turning points

title: How This 31 Year Old Woman Scammed JP Morgan
selection_reason: Young founder, media-made image, faked numbers to close a deal: the closest character analogue to McFarland among the channel's fraud videos.
topic: Charlie Javice / Frank and the JP Morgan acquisition (2021–2023)
narrative_question: Who was she and how did she manage to fool one of the biggest banks in the world?

hook.summary: Generic 'dream of success' framing over magazine covers, then the polished image vs. 'network of lies', a news clip about the charges, and the explicit question.
hook.promise: Who she was and how she fooled the bank.

structure.beat: Cold open: success myth, the facade, news clip of charges
Origin: first venture and media attention
The product explained (Frank, FAFSA), founder's own pitch clip
Red flags: regulator letter, NYT correction, Forbes 30u30
The deal: JP Morgan pitch, 4.25M customers claimed
Reveal: fewer than 300k real users
Fabrication heist: engineer refuses, professor builds fake data
Collapse: test email campaign exposes it, lawsuit
News clip + bank CEO quote
'Dig deeper': earlier lies about her past re-read with new eyes
Thesis: fake it till you make it, Holmes/SBF parallels, macro context
Personal opinion + outro

revelations: Fake list built by a hired professor (9:17)
Earlier venture and fellowship claims also false (13:07)
payoff: Verdict, then a second-pass reveal that the whole biography was a pattern, then a generational/macro thesis.

visual.method: histogram difference, frames 0.2 s apart, played at 4x; per-minute rate

archival_maps_graphics_3d: News segments, founder's own TV interviews, court/legal documents and web pages, stock city and office b-roll, black quote cards with italic serif text; no maps or 3D.

audio.voice: Same calm narrator, ~165 wpm (transcript count inflated by a duplicated panel, corrected estimate)
audio.ambience: News and interview clips as diegetic audio
audio.silence: Short pauses at section turns (1:22, 12:53) and at the outro
audio.transitions: Mostly hard cuts; channel ident at start

evidence: Direct quotes from the indictment/legal filings read aloud and shown as text, interviews with the fellowship's director, news clips. Sources not cited on screen in sampled frames.

thumbnail.composition: Candid photo of the subject outside court, white condensed text 'SHE STOLE $175 MILLION', red arrow, small handwritten 'Whoops', channel logo top-left.
thumbnail.title_relation: Thumbnail adds the number; title adds age and the victim (JP Morgan). Together they form one sentence.

works: Structured like a heist: claim, gap, fabrication, discovery
Second-pass reveal re-reads her early biography as a pattern
Uses the subject's own pitch clips as evidence against her
improve: Generic 'people dream of success' opening is slow compared with the specific charge
Ends with the narrator's personal opinion about a generation, which is not evidenced
transfer: After the fall, revisit earlier claims as a 'pattern' reveal (McFarland's Magnises before Fyre, NYC VIP after)
Use the subject's own promotional material as the 'claim' half of claim vs. reality

title: The Scammer Who Sold The Eiffel Tower (Twice)
selection_reason: Con-man biography with chaptered heists; shows how the mechanism of a con is explained step by step, and how a pre-film-era story is illustrated without footage of the subject.
topic: Victor Lustig (c. 1890–1947): money box con, Eiffel Tower sale, counterfeiting, Alcatraz
narrative_question: How did a broke petty thief become the most wanted man in the world?

hook.summary: In medias res: the subject on his way to Alcatraz, a bigger crime teased ('this wasn't even his most infamous scam'), the title promise ('sold the Eiffel Tower. Twice.').
hook.promise: The crazy true story of how a broke petty thief became the most wanted man in the world.

structure.beat: Flash-forward: Alcatraz
Ch.1 origin: uncertain identity, poverty, defining childhood scene
Ocean liner cons, reinvention as 'Count'
Ch.2 Magic Money Box: how the con worked, step by step
Plot twist: victim becomes partner and lover (foreshadowed downfall)
Sponsor
Ch.3 Eiffel Tower sale, step by step; why victims stay silent; second sale
Subscribe ask
Ch.4 Downfall: counterfeiting, Secret Service, betrayal tip, escape, Alcatraz
Ironic epitaph (death certificate), link to next video

revelations: The bribe request made the deal believable (14:15)
payoff: Returns to Alcatraz from the opening, ends on the ironic death certificate occupation.

visual.method: histogram difference, frames 0.2 s apart, played at 4x; per-minute rate

archival_maps_graphics_3d: Period photos animated as parallax collages; large 3D-looking place-name and keyword text composited into the scene (Alcatraz, Hostinné, Prague, 'Chapter 3', 'By 1925'); film footage with actors as illustration; flags; no maps.

audio.voice: One male narrator, ~206 wpm, punchy ('Twice.', 'here's the clever part', 'plot twist')
audio.music: Continuous bed, median about -17 dB, 0–1 % quiet
audio.silence: Music-only breaks of 11–18 s after the intro and at chapter turns (0:41, 5:48, 12:05, 16:31)

evidence: No primary documents or citations shown except a reproduced period banknote and signatures; uncertainties are stated in narration ('most likely born', 'there is a story that').

thumbnail.composition: Masked hooded figure (symbolic, not the subject) holding two Eiffel Towers with red price tags marked '?' and a dollar note; saturated sky background; no text.
thumbnail.title_relation: Thumbnail stages the title's action (selling the tower) without words; title carries the information.

works: Flash-forward to the prison, then rewind; closing callback to the same place
Each con explained as numbered mechanics with 'here's the clever part'
improve: Film footage with recognisable actors misleads about what is archival
Thumbnail uses an anachronistic hacker mask unrelated to a 1920s con man
transfer: Flash-forward opening and callback ending (Fyre: the empty FEMA tents, then rewind)
Mechanism walkthrough with on-screen numbered steps for how the money was raised
Place names as large text in the scene for geography (Exuma, Nassau, New York)
Say plainly when a fact is uncertain

title: Crazy Eddie's Crazy Fraud
selection_reason: Fraud behind a loud, beloved marketing image (hype vs. books); shows the channel's plain case-study structure.
topic: Crazy Eddie electronics chain: tax skimming in the 1970s, inflated profits after the 1984 IPO
narrative_question: How was an entire business a fraud for almost 20 years behind a fun, friendly brand?

hook.summary: First-person: the narrator chooses words to describe the case (deceptive, brilliant, scary, crazy) and states the thesis that the whole business was a fraud for almost 20 years.
hook.promise: Explain the layers of fraud in detail.

structure.beat: Personal framing: words for the case, thesis
Context: what the chain was (compared with Best Buy), peak numbers
The famous ads (clip), pop-culture echo, who the real Eddie was
Signpost slide: two opposite eras of fraud
Era 1: skimming cash to evade tax, advantage over competitors
Era 2: IPO, inflate profits; 'fraud by committing less fraud'
List of techniques: fake sales, inventory, timing, comparable-store sales
Why auditors missed it: the CFO cousin trained as an auditor
Collapse: takeover, bankruptcy, trials, flight to Israel
Epilogue: comeback attempt, death; personal reflection; comment prompt

revelations: Less skimming made profits look like growth (6:23)
The CFO was sent to college and into the audit firm (9:14)
payoff: Outcomes for each person, the failed internet comeback, and a return to the opening question about which word fits.

visual.method: histogram difference, frames 0.2 s apart, played at 4x; per-minute rate

archival_maps_graphics_3d: Simple bar charts (spreadsheet style), a recurring yellow 'agenda' slide in the subject's brand colour, scanned financial statements, dictionary screenshots, stock photos of cash and auditors, clips of the original TV ads; no maps or 3D.

audio.voice: First-person, conversational, ~202 wpm, opinions marked as such ('from my point of view')
audio.music: Low bed (median about -23.5 dB, lower than ColdFusion/Magnates at -17 to -19 dB)
audio.ambience: Original ad audio and court interview clips inserted
audio.transitions: Hard cuts; slide returns as chapter marker

evidence: Shows scanned financial statements and charts of skimming/sales by year; quotes and TV clips of the participants; no visible citations.

thumbnail.composition: Brand's own yellow, the logo lettering 'CRAZY EDDIE', black-and-white cut-out of the founder with thumbs up, red stamp 'SCANDAL'.
thumbnail.title_relation: Thumbnail = brand + verdict; title adds the pun ('Crazy Fraud').

works: A recurring agenda slide tells the viewer where they are in a two-part fraud
Explains accounting tricks with everyday analogies (cash under the mattress)
Plays the subject's own ads so the viewer feels the hype first
improve: Low visual variety (long holds on stock photos and slides)
transfer: A recurring 'map' graphic that returns at each act (e.g. Fyre timeline: promo, sales, island, collapse, trials)
Let the viewer experience the hype through the subject's own marketing before the reveal
Explain financial mechanics with one concrete analogy each

title: The Bernie Madoff Scandal - A Simple Overview
selection_reason: Explains a fraud mechanism to non-experts through a role-played victim perspective; directly reusable for explaining Fyre ticket buyers' and investors' point of view.
narrative_question: What actually happened, and how did he get away with it for so long?

hook.summary: Opinionated first line ('I don't like this guy'), acknowledges the viewer has heard the term but may not understand it, promises a decent overview.
hook.promise: A simple, understandable overview of a complicated scandal.

structure.beat: Opinion + gap in viewer's understanding
Role-play: narrator as a 2004 investor, the referral, the meeting, steady returns
Switch perspective: what Madoff actually did (bank account, fake reports)
Ponzi context (Charles Ponzi)
How he got away with it: numbered list (charisma, reputation, believable 10–12 %, consistency, paperwork, SEC ignored the whistleblower)
Collapse in 2008: withdrawals exceed deposits; sons turn him in
Family question, sentence, aftermath
Victims and victim fund
Lessons, film recommendation, joke pre-emption, comment prompt

revelations: No stocks were ever bought; reports typed in the office (2:24)
payoff: 2008 run on the fund exposes the scheme; human cost and the small share recovered.

visual.method: histogram difference, frames 0.2 s apart, played at 4x; per-minute rate

archival_maps_graphics_3d: Stock footage acted out to match the role-play (handshake, phone, money case), news photos and clips, big-word cards ('How?', '12%', 'Made off'), a meme image for an aside; no charts, maps or 3D.

audio.voice: First-person host voice, ~183 wpm, jokes and asides
audio.ambience: One news clip with the sons' statement

evidence: Mostly narration; a news clip and a DOJ victim-fund web page; numbers stated, not sourced on screen.

thumbnail.composition: Black field, title text 'THE BERNIE MADOFF' with red 'SCANDAL' stamp, cut-out photo of Madoff with banknotes, subtitle 'A SIMPLE OVERVIEW'.
thumbnail.title_relation: Thumbnail repeats the title almost word for word (series template).

works: Viewer lives the scam as a victim before the reveal
'How did he get away with it' answered as a clear numbered list
Humour asides lighten a dark topic without mocking victims
improve: Very low visual variety; stock footage literalises the narration
Thumbnail duplicates the title instead of adding information
Recommends an outside film without adding context
transfer: Second-person role-play: 'it's early 2017, you see the orange tile on Instagram...' then 'here's what was actually happening'
Numbered 'why it worked' list after the reveal
Ending that turns to victims and recovery figures
